Reproducing Semenov et al. (2026) from dandiset 001516¶

Paper. Semenov I, Silkuniene G, Silkunas M, Pakhomova ON, Bixler JN, Ibey BL, Kochunov P, Pakhomov AG (2026). Sub-microsecond optical measurements of cell membrane charging and lesioning by pulsed electric fields. Bioelectrochemistry 171, 109283. doi:10.1016/j.bioelechem.2026.109283. The claims file was written from the version of record (main text, Methods, Results, Discussion and the legends of Figures 1 to 7; the paper names no supplement and links no code).

Dandiset. DANDI:001516, "Plasma Membrane Recovery of Cells Following 1 us Electroporation Pulse", version 0.261006.1833. Why this version: the paper cites no dandiset version (its data statement reads "Data will be made available on request"), and 0.261006.1833 is the only published version, so it is the most recent one. The draft has the same 72 assets and size; it was not used, as a draft can change.

Claims. claims/001516/10.1016-j.bioelechem.2026.109283.yaml, 32 claims. What the dataset holds (the data check below): 72 image sets from 12 fields of view recorded on 2023-06-22, all stained with FluoVolt, with 1.00-mm electrodes, 20 sham frames and 40 pulse frames per set, single pulses or pulse pairs at 50 to 250 V (described as 0.15 to 1.57 kV/cm) and pair intervals of 1, 5, 25, 125 and 250 us (the description lists four intervals, without 250 us). None of the paper's experiments is among them: Figures 1, 2B to 2D, 4B to 4D, 5 and 7 used Di-8-ANEPPS, Figures 2A and 4A a FluoVolt escalation from 43 to 1400 V/cm in sets of 40 and 60 images with 1.6-mm electrodes, Figure 3 the 43 to 360 V/cm sets of both dyes, and Figure 6 Fluo-4 calcium imaging. Only the one claim that is a computation from Eq. (2), with no recordings, can be tested.

Claims Tested here Outcome
fig5b-conductivity-calibration (Eq. 2, no recordings) yes see its section
fig1, fig2b, fig2c, fig2d, fig4b, fig4c, fig4d, fig5a, fig5c (Di-8-ANEPPS, 1-us and 0.3-us escalations, Gd3+) no blocked, data missing
fig2a, fig3, fig4a (FluoVolt and Di-8-ANEPPS escalations from 43 to 1400 V/cm) no blocked, data missing
fig6a, fig6b (Fluo-4 calcium imaging) no blocked, data missing
fig7a, fig7b, fig7ab, fig7c (two-pulse recovery, Di-8-ANEPPS, n = 5) no blocked, data missing

The last section measures the dataset's own FluoVolt sets with the paper's method, to show what they hold; it decides no claim.

Data check¶

Each file was streamed and reduced as it loaded: per cell found in the field, the 6-pixel-wide perimeter trace of every frame (360 points). Each check of the metadata against the values is stated under its output.

There is one ImageSeries per file, StrobeImaging, 60 frames of 512 x 512 uint16 pixels at 6 Hz, and nothing else: no stimulus, epoch or trial table, no processing module, no pixel size. The 12 "subjects" are fields of view; the pulse protocol of each set is only in the free text of session_description. One pixel in one file is near the 14-bit ceiling and none near a measured cell, so saturation does not affect the measures. Every field of view has six sets: a sham and five single pulses (c6, c7), or six pulse pairs at one interval (two fields per interval), so the description's single and paired protocols are all present, with 2 fields of view per protocol.

Distinct general descriptions: 1
 The experimental protocol consisted of two parts. First, cells were exposed to asingle pulse at various electric field strengths ranging from 0.15 to 1.57 kV/cm (0.15, 0.52, 0.9, 1.27, 1.57). Second, cells were exposed to a pair of pulses. The first pulse varied in amplitude using the same field strengths as in the single pulse protocol, while the second pulse was always maintained at 0.15 kV/cm. The inter-pulse interval varied across 1, 5, 25, and 125 µs. For dual-pulse experiments, fluorescence imaging was timed to capture the response 0.9 µs after the onset of the second pulse. All experiments were performed in standard physiological solution containing (in mM): 140 NaCl, 5.4 KCl, 2 CaCl2, 1.5 MgCl2, 10 D-glucose, and 10 HEPES (pH 7.3, 290-300 mOsm/kg). CHO cells were seeded in culture dishes with 20 mm glass window 1 h before the experiment to maintain spherical shape. More method d

All 72 files name FluoVolt with a FITC filter cube, and 1.00-mm electrodes. The paper's two-pulse experiment (Fig. 7) used Di-8-ANEPPS and its electrodes were 1.6 mm apart (Methods 2.2). Within each field of view the first-pulse amplitude rises from 0 to 250 V across the six sets, except c1, whose 50-V pair was recorded before its sham pair. The test pulse is always 50 V, which the description gives as 0.15 kV/cm, the paper's 150 V/cm test pulse. The description lists the field strengths 0.15, 0.52, 0.9, 1.27 and 1.57 kV/cm for 50 to 250 V; the files give no mapping, so the list is read in order. The general description gives the intervals as "1, 5, 25, and 125 us", but fields c5 and c12 hold pairs at 250 us. The field mapping is not proportional to voltage (5 times the voltage for 10.5 times the field), while the paper states that the current scaled linearly with voltage (Methods 2.2); it is checked against the responses below.

small = {}
for s in sets:
    small.setdefault(P.fov(s["subject"]), []).append(s["mean_img_small"].ravel().astype(float))
def zs(v):
    return (v - v.mean()) / v.std()
within = [np.mean(zs(a) * zs(b)) for v in small.values() for a, b in zip(v[:-1], v[1:])]
keys = list(small)
fovmean = {k: zs(np.mean(v, 0)) for k, v in small.items()}

No array is deposited twice. Consecutive sets of one field of view are near-identical images (the same cells), while different fields of view correlate at most moderately (the shared illumination profile), so the 12 fields of view are 12 distinct recordings. starting_time holds the Unix time of each set's acquisition, the same instant as its session_start_time, so in NWB terms every recording starts about 53 years after its session starts; NWB defines starting_time relative to the session's reference time, so this is a format error. Each file has its own session_start_time (the set's time), although all share the session id session_2023-06-22.

Touching cells are split (c2, c3, c10 and c12 each hold a touching pair), and objects that are not round are left out (listed above: a stacked pair and a cluster of dim cells in c11, and small or elongated objects in c4 to c7), as are objects not found in every set of the field of view. This leaves 2 or 3 cells per field of view, 29 in all, each found in all six sets, with centroids that move by at most 4.6 pixels between sets, so each cell is the same cell across its sets. The files do not say which cell was the experiment's cell (the paper used one cell per experiment, and the subject ids, c1 to c12, name a field of view), so the measures below use every kept cell and break the results down by field of view. Radii are in pixels: the files give no pixel size, so the radius in um that Eq. (1) needs cannot be computed from them.

The field direction is not recorded. It is taken from the data: the first angular harmonic of dF points the same way in every field of view, 82 to 92 degrees (image up), which is then the cathode-facing pole (the pole that brightens, Methods 2.3). Taking the direction from the response that is then measured is circular, so each set's poles are placed with the direction pooled over the other pulse sets of its field of view only; it differs from the pooled direction by -0.4 to 0.7 degrees, far less than the +-5 degree pole arc. All of this is used only in the descriptive sections, which decide no claim.

# Placement of the trace: every measured cell, in its 250-V (1570 V/cm) set, full-resolution mean image
show = [(s, c) for s in sets if s["kind"] != "sham" and s["v1"] == 250 for c in s["cells"]]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 8, figsize=(20, 10.5))
phi = np.deg2rad(np.arange(P.N_ANG) + 0.5)
for ax in axes.ravel():
    ax.axis("off")
for ax, (s, c) in zip(axes.ravel(), show):
    y0, x0 = c["crop_origin"]
    ax.imshow(c["crop"], cmap="gray")
    for r, col in [(c["edge_r"], "tab:red"), (c["edge_r"] - P.TRACE_WIDTH, "tab:cyan")]:
        ax.plot(c["cx"] - x0 + np.cos(phi) * r, c["cy"] - y0 - np.sin(phi) * r, c=col, lw=0.7)
    a = np.deg2rad(P.angle_of(loo, s))
    ax.plot([c["cx"] - x0, c["cx"] - x0 + np.cos(a) * c["r_eq"]], [c["cy"] - y0, c["cy"] - y0 - np.sin(a) * c["r_eq"]], c="yellow", lw=1)
    ax.set_title(f"{P.fov(s['subject'])} cell {c['cell_id']}", fontsize=9)
fig.suptitle("Trace between the red (outer edge) and cyan lines; yellow: cathode-facing direction")
plt.show()
edge = np.concatenate([c["edge_r"] / c["r_eq"] for s in sets for c in s["cells"]])
print(f"{len(show)} cells shown. Outer edge of the trace over all cells, sets and angles: {edge.min():.2f} to {edge.max():.2f} "
      f"equivalent radii; at the 0.7 lower bound of the search: {100 * np.mean(edge <= 0.705):.1f}% of angles, "
      f"at the 1.4 upper bound: {100 * np.mean(edge >= 1.395):.1f}%")

29 cells shown. Outer edge of the trace over all cells, sets and angles: 0.70 to 1.36 equivalent radii; at the 0.7 lower bound of the search: 4.4% of angles, at the 1.4 upper bound: 0.0%

The trace lies on the bright membrane ring just inside each cell's outer edge. Where a cell touches another (the split pairs in c2, c3, c10 and c12, and c11 cell 1, which touches a cell that is left out), the rays stop at the boundary between the two, and the trace follows the contact; it has small notches where a neighbour or the image border is close (c1 cell 2, c11 cell 1). At 4.4% of angles the edge sits at the lower bound of the search (0.7 equivalent radii), and the 15-degree median filter along the perimeter smooths these. The paper drew its trace by hand, so the placement differs from the paper's in any case.

scan = []
for s in sets:
    for c in s["cells"]:
        a = P.log_asym(c["trace"], P.angle_of(loo, s))
        t = [abs(stats.ttest_ind(a[:k], a[k:]).statistic) for k in range(5, 56)]
        label = "sham" if s["kind"] == "sham" else ("pair, 0 V first" if (s["kind"] == "pair" and s["v1"] == 0) else s["kind"])
        scan.append({"fov": P.fov(s["subject"]), "protocol": label, "best_split": 5 + int(np.argmax(t)),
                     "step_at_20": 100 * (a[20:].mean() - a[:20].mean()),
                     "step_within_baseline": 100 * (a[10:20].mean() - a[:10].mean())})
scan = pd.DataFrame(scan)
print("Frame after which the cathode/anode log ratio changes most (frames are numbered from 0; 20 = after the 20 sham frames),")
print("number of cell-sets per protocol:")
print(pd.crosstab(scan.protocol, scan.best_split).to_string())
print("\nStep of the log ratio x 100, frames 20-59 minus 0-19, and the null step within the baseline (frames 10-19 minus 0-9):")
print(scan.groupby("protocol")[["step_at_20", "step_within_baseline"]].agg(["mean", "min", "max"]).round(1).to_string())

The 20 sham frames come first. In the pulse sets the polar contrast changes after frame 20 (frames counted from 0) in 168 of 170 cell-sets with a pulse, and the step is 12 to 77 (log ratio x 100); in the sham sets the best split is elsewhere and the step is -1.2 to 0.3, and inside the baseline, where nothing changes, it is -1.9 to 6.9. This contrast between conditions shows that the frames and the pulse protocol share one clock, and that the description's 20 sham and 40 pulse exposures are the order of the frames.

The collapsed profiles carry a uniform offset: on the cells, the last 40 frames are dimmer than baseline frames 1 to 19 by 13.3 to 16.2% in the sham sets, with no pulse, so the offset is not a field response. The whole image dims less (median ratio 0.97), so the cells' dye fades more than the background, consistent with bleaching. The first frame is also dimmer, below 0.9 of frames 1 to 19 in 65 of the 72 files (median 0.64, range 0.52 to 1.11), so F0 is taken from frames 1 to 19 here (a deviation: the paper uses every baseline image). Keeping frame 0 in F0, as the paper's method would, gives a sham offset of -9.4 to -16.8% and shifts the single-pulse pole values by about 3 points at the cathodic pole (-14.7 against -11.9%) and 2 at the anodic pole (-43.3 against -41.7%). The paper's measure does not remove the offset, and it shifts both poles equally. The flash-to-flash variation of the whole image is about 4% (median s.d. over mean), which the paper says collapsing the frames is meant to average out. The sham sets have almost no first harmonic, as expected without a field.

The response at 100 V is 1.36 to 1.85 times that at 50 V. This is closer to a field proportional to voltage (2.0) than to the listed fields (3.47), but FluoVolt saturates (Results 3.2), which compresses the ratio, so the mapping of amplitudes to field strengths cannot be checked from the data and is used as the description gives it.

The paper's Discussion names this dataset's design as future work: "Future studies should focus on the time course of membrane recovery, perhaps using the same two-pulse protocol as in Fig. 7, but varying the time interval between the pulses." The dataset does not hold the recordings behind any of the paper's figures.

fig5b-conductivity-calibration¶

By Eq. (2), the effective membrane conductivity barely affects charging while it stays far below cytosol and medium conductivities; a 10-fold rise reduces IMP by about 2% and a 100-fold rise by 12%.

Criterion: a computation from Eq. (2) with the constants of Methods 2.3 (lambda_i 0.4 S/m, lambda_o 1.64 S/m, R 8 um, d 5 nm, intact lambda_m 3e-7 S/m); the reduction is relative to IMPC, readings (a) 1 - f/1.5 and (b) 1 - f(lambda_m)/f(3e-7 S/m). Reproduced when both values are within tolerance (2 +- 0.2% and 12 +- 1.2%) under one reading. It uses no recordings.

f0 = P.lambda_f(lam0)
print(f"f at the intact conductivity 3e-7 S/m: {f0:.6f} (1.5 for a non-conducting membrane)")

for fold in [10, 100]:
    f = P.lambda_f(lam0 * fold)
    res.append({"fold": fold, "lambda_m_S_per_m": f"{lam0 * fold:.0e}", "f": f,
                "reduction_a_pct (1 - f/1.5)": 100 * (1 - f / 1.5),
                "reduction_b_pct (1 - f/f0)": 100 * (1 - f / f0)})
res = pd.DataFrame(res)
print(res.round(4).to_string(index=False))
exp = {10: (2, 0.2), 100: (12, 1.2)}
for reading in ["reduction_a_pct (1 - f/1.5)", "reduction_b_pct (1 - f/f0)"]:
    ok = [abs(r[reading] - exp[r.fold][0]) <= exp[r.fold][1] for _, r in res.iterrows()]
    print(f"{reading}: 10-fold within 2 +- 0.2: {ok[0]}; 100-fold within 12 +- 1.2: {ok[1]}")

      f"(reading b): {folds[np.argmin(abs(100 * (1 - P.lambda_f(lam0 * folds) / f0) - 2))]:.1f}")

Result: not reproduced. Eq. (2) with the Methods' constants gives a 1.33% IMP reduction for a 10-fold rise in effective conductivity under reading (a) and 1.20% under reading (b), outside 2 +- 0.2%; a 100-fold rise gives 11.87% and 11.75%, within 12 +- 1.2%. A 2% reduction needs a 15- to 16-fold rise. In the variant grid the 10-fold value is 0.60 to 2.46%, and within 2 +- 0.2% only for a 10-um radius with a 4-nm membrane (2.06%) or a 12-um radius with a 5-nm membrane (1.98%), not with the stated 8 um and 5 nm. The printed points of the Eq. (2) curve (measured IMP 98.67% of IMPC at 10-fold, 88.13% at 100-fold, 42.62% at 1000-fold, 6.91% at 10000-fold) can be set against the curve of Fig. 5B to see whether the paper drew it with the same constants; the notebook does not read the figure.

What the dataset holds, measured with the paper's method (no claim is decided here)¶

These are the dataset's own FluoVolt experiments, which the paper does not report. They are measured with the paper's collapsed pole measure (Methods 2.3) so that the record shows what the data hold and how close they come to the paper's Fig. 7 design. They are not the paper's data (dye, field strengths, electrode spacing and cell numbers differ), so they decide no outcome. Two versions are shown: the paper's measure (cath, anod), and the same with the profile's uniform offset removed (cath_c, anod_c), since the sham sets show that offset is not a field response. Cells of one field of view were recorded together, so fields of view, not cells, are the independent experiments.

With single pulses the FluoVolt response at the poles, offset removed, does not grow beyond 520 V/cm: the cathodic response is 14.3 and 15.3% at 150 and 520 V/cm, 7.0 and 9.0% at 900 and 1270 V/cm, and 15.6% at 1570 V/cm; the anodic response peaks at -23.2% at 520 V/cm and is -13.8 to -14.6% above it, with c6 and c7 far apart (-2.6 to -3.8% in c6 against -23.9 to -26.6% in c7 at 900 V/cm and above). This resembles the pattern the paper reports for FluoVolt (saturation, then a smaller response), at smaller values than the paper's 66 to 71% and -83%; the files give no pixel size and no calibration, and the trace placement differs from the paper's hand-drawn trace, so the sizes are not comparable. These are 4 cells in 2 fields of view.

In [11]:
# Variant for fig2a-fluovolt-stable (decides no outcome): stability within the dataset's own FluoVolt sets
# (c6, c7). Per-frame pole dF against F0 (frames 1-19); start and end of the 40 pulse frames and of the
# baseline under the criterion's readings, with frame 0 left out of the baseline (and kept, as a check).
win = {"pulse (a): frame 20 vs 59": (slice(20, 21), slice(59, 60)),
       "pulse (b): frames 20-29 vs 50-59": (slice(20, 30), slice(50, 60)),
       "baseline (a): frame 1 vs 19": (slice(1, 2), slice(19, 20)),
       "baseline (b): frames 1-9 vs 10-19": (slice(1, 10), slice(10, 20)),
       "baseline (a), frame 0 kept: 0 vs 19": (slice(0, 1), slice(19, 20)),
       "baseline (b), frame 0 kept: 0-9 vs 10-19": (slice(0, 10), slice(10, 20))}
rows = []
for s in sets:
    if s["kind"] == "pair":
        continue
    for c in s["cells"]:
        for pole, x in zip(["cathodic", "anodic"], P.pole_frames(c["trace"], P.angle_of(loo, s))):
            for w, (a, b) in win.items():
                rows.append(dict(fov=P.fov(s["subject"]), cell=c["cell_id"], E1=P.field_of(s["v1"]), pole=pole, window=w,
                                 change=x[b].mean() - x[a].mean(), start=x[a].mean(), end=x[b].mean()))
st = pd.DataFrame(rows)
def paired(g):
    return pd.Series({"cells": len(g), "change_mean": g.change.mean(), "change_min": g.change.min(),
                      "change_max": g.change.max(), "p_paired_t": stats.ttest_rel(g.end, g.start).pvalue})
res = st.groupby(["window", "E1", "pole"], sort=False).apply(paired, include_groups=False)
print(f"End minus start of per-frame pole dF (percentage points of F0), 2-tailed paired t-test over the {st.groupby(['fov', 'cell']).ngroups} cells of c6 and c7:")
print(res.round(3).to_string())
print("\nPer field of view, mean change (points), sets at 1270 and 1570 V/cm (the dataset's levels of 1000 V/cm and above):")
print(st[st.E1 >= 1000].pivot_table(index=["window", "E1", "pole"], columns="fov", values="change", sort=False).round(1).to_string())

The dataset's own single-pulse sets do not show the stability that fig2a-fluovolt-stable states for the paper's cells (this decides no outcome; they are not the paper's cells). Over the 40 pulse frames the per-frame pole dF falls in every set, the sham set included (-12.1 and -12.2 points under reading (b), p = 0.001 or less, 4 cells), so the fall is not a field effect. At the dataset's two levels above 1000 V/cm (1270 and 1570 V/cm) it falls by 2.9 to 11.1 points under reading (b) (p 0.003 to 0.066; 3 of 4 pole-sets at p < 0.05), and by 3.8 to 24.0 points under reading (a) (p 0.024 to 0.76; 1 of 4 at p < 0.05), where a single frame carries the ~4% flash-to-flash noise. The baseline falls too, by 16.3 and 15.9 points in the sham set under reading (b) (frames 1-9 against 10-19); with frame 0 kept, frame 0 against frame 19 differs by 12 to 78 points, the first-frame dimming. Under both readings at least one pole-set at 1270 or 1570 V/cm and the sham-set baselines change at p < 0.05, so the claim's rule applied to these recordings would give not reproduced; this is a property of these recordings, not a test of the paper's.

pr = pt[pt.kind == "pair"].copy()
def pct_of_control(df, col):
    t = df.pivot_table(index=["interval_us", "fov", "cell"], columns="E1", values=col)
    return 100 * t.div(t[150.0], axis=0)

In the paper's measure the cathodic value at the 150/150 control is small (4.5%) next to the uniform offset it contains (-10.1%), so its percentages vary widely between cells (-941 to 1074%). With the offset removed, the cathodic test-pulse response at the 5-us interval is 90 to 92% of the control (mean over cells) after conditioning at 520 and 900 V/cm, 76% after 1270 V/cm and 68% after 1570 V/cm; the anodic response falls less, to 93% and 90%. In the paper's measure the anodic pole falls to 70% and 64%. This resembles the paper's Fig. 7B (bottom), in another dye and with 5 cells in two fields of view.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 6, figsize=(18, 3), sharey=True)
ang = np.arange(P.N_ANG) + 0.5
lo, hi = np.inf, -np.inf
profiles = {}
for s in sets:
    if s["kind"] == "pair" and s["interval_us"] == 5:
        for c in s["cells"]:
            df = P.profile_df(c["trace"])
            # rotate so that index k is the angle k + 0.5 degrees from the cathode-facing pole
            profiles.setdefault(s["v1"], []).append(np.roll(df - df.mean(), -int(round(P.angle_of(loo, s) - 0.5))))
for ax, v in zip(axes, sorted(profiles)):
    m = np.mean(profiles[v], 0)
    lo, hi = min(lo, m.min()), max(hi, m.max())
    ax.plot(ang, m)
    ax.axhline(0, c="gray", lw=0.5)
    ax.set_title(f"{P.field_of(v):.0f}/150 V/cm")
    ax.set_xlabel("angle from cathode (deg)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("dF, offset removed (%)")
fig.suptitle(f"5-us pairs, mean profile over the {len(profiles[0])} cells of c2 and c9")
plt.show()
print(f"Plotted range: {lo:.1f} to {hi:.1f}%")

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's: the one tested claim is a computation that uses no data, run as the claims file gives it. The variant measures of the dataset's own experiments place the 6-pixel trace automatically inside the outer edge of each cell, take the field direction from the data (for each set, from the other sets of its field of view), use every round cell in a field of view, leave the dimmed frame 0 out of F0, and collapse 20 and 40 frames in place of 40 and 60.

What was found about the dataset:

  • It does not hold the data of any of the paper's figures. It holds a FluoVolt two-pulse experiment with intervals of 1 to 250 us and fields of 150 to 1570 V/cm, recorded with 1.00-mm electrodes in sets of 20 sham and 40 pulse frames, which the paper does not report (its Discussion names it as future work); its metadata names the paper as the publication of these data.
  • The general description gives the intervals as 1, 5, 25 and 125 us; two fields of view are at 250 us.
  • The pulse protocol of each set is only in free text; there is no stimulus or trial table. The 20/40 frame order is confirmed by the data.
  • The field direction, the pixel size and which cell of a field of view is the experiment's cell are not recorded; the 12 subjects are fields of view, each with 2 or 3 whole, round cells measured here (29 in all).
  • The listed field strengths (0.15 to 1.57 kV/cm for 50 to 250 V) are not proportional to voltage, and the files do not map amplitudes to fields.
  • starting_time is the Unix time of the acquisition, not an offset from session_start_time.
  • On the cells, the pulse frames are 13 to 16% dimmer than sham frames 1 to 19 even in sham sets, a uniform offset that the paper's measure does not remove, and the per-frame pole dF falls within the pulse frames and within the baseline of the sham sets.
  • In 65 of the 72 files the first frame is more than 10% dimmer than frames 1 to 19 (median 0.64, range 0.52 to 1.11 over files).
